analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in steps to $6.65 and applies it to the Northern Mariana Islands.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 2001 with 36 Senate cosponsors, the bill never got a committee hearing or vote and died when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.75 within 30 days of passage, then to $6.25 in 2002 and $6.65 in 2003. It would also have applied federal wage rules to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands for the first time, phasing that territory's wage up to the federal level in 50-cent steps every six months. The bill went to the Senate labor committee and was never heard from again.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum wage, who would have seen their hourly pay rise from $5.15 to as much as $6.65 by 2003, a raise of about 29% over two years.

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.75 an hour beginning 30 days after enactment, to $6.25 during 2002, and to $6.65 beginning January 1, 2003.

It applies federal minimum wage law to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands for the first time, raising that territory's wage from $3.55 by 50 cents every six months until it reaches the federal level.

analysis.who_pays: Labor-intensive employers — restaurants, retail, and hotels chief among them — who would pay higher hourly wages, and garment manufacturers in the Northern Mariana Islands, who would lose their exemption from federal wage law.

drawbacks.text: Higher wage floors raise labor costs for small businesses and labor-intensive industries, and opponents argued the increases could reduce hours or entry-level jobs; the bill contained no tax credits or offsets for affected employers.
The staged increases (to $6.65 in 2003) were set in the bill itself rather than indexed to inflation, so the raise's value would erode unless Congress acted again.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A roughly 29% raise over two years is a large, direct benefit to workers at the wage floor, while the cost is spread across many employers in the form of higher wages. The absence of any offsetting relief for small businesses was a fair criticism, but the main drawbacks are the ordinary trade-offs of any minimum wage increase, not a design defect unique to this bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate labor committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or a vote there, and expired with the 107th Congress.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy of Massachusetts introduced the bill on February 7, 2001, joined by 25 fellow Democrats listed on introduction.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
36 of the Senate's 49 Democrats cosponsored the bill; the action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — for the rest of the Congress.
No Republican senator cosponsored, and the bill died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, never having reached the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay at or near the federal minimum wage kept the $5.15 rate in place, which Congress had not raised since 1997.

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and gave introductory remarks when it was introduced.

for.name: 36 of 49 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it the support of most of the Senate's Democratic caucus.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction that received the bill by referral
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on February 7, 2001 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 36 cosponsors were Senate Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never advanced far enough for a floor vote that would have shown a full party split.

industries.note: These employers would have paid $1.50 more per hour by 2003 for their lowest-wage workers. Their interest in keeping the wage frozen ran directly against the raise that workers at the floor would have received.

industries.industry: Garment and other manufacturers in the Northern Mariana Islands
industries.note: The islands had been exempt from federal minimum wage law and paid far less; the bill would have phased that out. The exemption's value came from paying wages well below the federal floor.
